title: [Bug]: No more files after update to 28.0.2
body:
### ⚠️ This issue respects the following points: ⚠️

- [X] This is a **bug**, not a question or a configuration/webserver/proxy issue.
- [X] This issue is **not** already reported on [Github](https://github.com/nextcloud/server/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3Abug) OR [Nextcloud Community Forum](https://<redacted-host>/) _(I've searched it)_.
- [X] Nextcloud Server **is** up to date. See [Maintenance and Release Schedule](https://github.com/nextcloud/server/wiki/Maintenance-and-Release-Schedule) for supported versions.
- [X] I agree to follow Nextcloud's [Code of Conduct](https://nextcloud.com/contribute/code-of-conduct/).

### Bug description

After the update from 28.0.1 to 28.0.2, the group folders in the files were no longer displayed. Instead of the "New" button, there was an "Add" button. However, the button could not be clicked, so I rule out a Groupfolders problem as it generally no longer worked. After going back to 28.0.1 and a DB restore it works again and files can be uploaded again. The behavior is the same with php8.2 and php8.3.

### Steps to reproduce

1. update from 28.0.1 to 28.0.2
2. open Nextcloud Files in the browser
3. an "Add" button (up to 28.0.1 "New") is displayed
4. the button cannot be clicked and no new files or folders can be created


### Expected behavior

The group folders should be displayed and you should be able to create new folders or files using the "Add" button.

### Installation method

Community Manual installation with Archive

### Nextcloud Server version

28

### Operating system

Debian/Ubuntu

### PHP engine version

PHP 8.3

### Web server

Nginx

### Database engine version

MariaDB

### Is this bug present after an update or on a fresh install?

Updated from a MINOR version (ex. 22.1 to 22.2)

### Are you using the Nextcloud Server Encryption module?

Encryption is Disabled

### What user-backends are you using?

- [X] Default user-backend _(database)_
- [ ] LDAP/ Active Directory
- [ ] SSO - SAML
- [ ] Other

comments.author: participant7
comments.body:
> With this statement, no one will use current versions in the future. 

All three of the major versions I mentioned (v26, v27, v28) are "current versions". What major version to upgrade to and how aggressively to do so is a local/sysadmin decision. The Nextcloud project supports 2-3 major versions at the same time, with the earlier two always being the most mature/field tested.

I'm a sysadmin myself (and also a volunteer within the project). I was pointing out that if you don't have a strategy in place for testing in your specific environment and/or at least having a rollback approach, then perhaps you should explore your update strategy and/or upgrade less aggressively. All supported major versions receive bug fixes and security fixes so there's no downside in many cases to sitting on the middle supported major version (or even the oldest if you prefer to be conservative).

If you want to run the latest major release, well, that's great too. It's entirely up to you.

It's no different than deciding which version of a major Linux distribution to run, even though multiple major versions are supported simultaneously. There are always trade-offs to running the latest/least field tested of any software.

> We should be able to expect that if a bug breaks Nextcloud, a hotfix or patch will be released. That was the case in the past.

The code with the fix is there in the links already mentioned just as is always the case:

- participant13://github.com/nextcloud/server/pull/43318
- participant13://github.com/nextcloud-libraries/nextcloud-files/pull/882

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
The conversation is not necessarily very productive as it stands, and I do not think me intervening is going to change anything, but I really take issue with the way user complaints are handled.

I was under the impression, correct me if I am wrong, that the Nextcloud project versioning followed the [semantic versioning convention](participant13://semver.org/). Since this bug was introduced between 28.0.1 and 28.0.2, it means it was introduced at a patch level, hence, running 26.x.x or 27.x.x seemingly wouldn't have shielded anyone from such a bug being introduced.

Now things happen obviously, no process is ever foolproof, this is bound to happen at some point. But expecting users to deploy a full testing arsenal just to check for obscure edge cases even the developers couldn't catch on their own is not realistic.

Moreover, as said above, there are also cases where roll-backing is impossible, either because no backups where made, or because affected users took too long to report the issue, causing too large of a gap in db state. For these users, no solution is provided besides waiting for the next patch a few weeks from now. It really sucks 😞.

I think this issue highlights a longstanding issue with the way Nextcloud handles updates and rollbacks. Ideally there should not be any issue downgrading from one patch level to another, following semver, yet this is not supported.

I know this is not something that ought to change in the short term, but I really wish this could be ironed out. In my case, this has not been the first time I had to rollback, and it is *always* a chore, even with my single user instance. I can not even begin to imagine how annoying and unnecessarily stressful it has to be at a larger scale.

Anyway guys, I know users complaining when they **should** have been more cautious is never great to read, and I really want to stress that I love the software, I really do! I really hope my message did not come as condescending or insulting or whatever, I am just sincerely hoping for a better process for situations like these.

Peace ✌️

comments.author: participant7
comments.body:
> I was under the impression, correct me if I am wrong, that the Nextcloud project versioning followed the semantic versioning convention. 

As much as anything does, sure.

> Since this bug was introduced between 28.0.1 and 28.0.2, it means it was introduced at a patch level, hence, running 26.x.x or 27.x.x seemingly wouldn't have shielded anyone from such a bug being introduced

I know of nothing in semantic versioning that suggests that minor/patch levels are symmetrical across major versions. You can't compare the minor or patch levels across major version boundaries.

That wouldn't make much sense: after all major versions introduce breaking changes and new APIs. The bugs that arise in new major versions often can't exist in older major release trees because they don't even share the same code.

So running 26.y.z /27.y.z absolutely would have shielded anyone from this bug. That was my point. 

This bug exists because 28 is a newer tree. It was introduced in 28 due to substantial breaking changes that were introduced with a new major version. You won't encounter it in a 26 or 27 release (unless we screw up). 

There's no need to fix this bug in the 26 and 27 code trees because the code in question doesn't exist there. Those are frozen branches outside of critical bug fixes and security updates. And we take the time and the effort to keep them maintained with those critical fixes for the time posted on the schedule I shared previously (participant13://github.com/nextcloud/server/wiki/Maintenance-and-Release-Schedule#currently-maintained-versions) - which is at least a year.

> In my case, this has not been the first time I had to rollback, and it is always a chore, even with my single user instance. I can not even begin to imagine how annoying and unnecessarily stressful it has to be at a larger scale.

In my experience, large installations rarely run the latest and greatest of anything (and if they do: it's a deliberate decision, taken for a compelling reason, and done with eyes wide open, and extra preparedness).

Look everybody has different comfort levels - I personally run 26.y.z (going on 27.y.z this month) in production even though I'm doing development and support for >=v28. LOL. I prefer significant stability and as much predictability as possible when it comes to my data. Nothing beats lots of field time for that!

I continue to be baffled when people deploy a bleeding edge major release (not yet 60 days old) and want it to behave like the older mature/ battle tested majors (which still routinely - albeit conservatively - receive patches for critical newly discovered bugs as needed!). 

There's a reason all three majors coexist - we don't just maintain all three for the fun of it! :-)

Everybody has different needs, wants, and preferences.

I know some people will *always* install the latest. And that's cool. I'm like that too - just not in my production environment for certain things... Like file storage. :-)

Btw: I'm not necessarily in disagreement with the rest of your comments and ideas. But they take work and we should move this discussion to a dedicated issue or the forum - or a bit of both. :-)
